content: The scientific literature on treatments for opioid dependence in adults strongly supports the use of pharmacotherapy as a necessary and acceptable component of care. However, there is a lack of systematic reviews assessing the effectiveness of pharmacological maintenance treatments specifically for adolescents. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of maintenance treatments, either alone or in combination with psychosocial interventions, compared to no intervention, other pharmacological treatments, or psychosocial interventions. The outcomes assessed included treatment retention, reduction in substance use, and improvements in health and social functioning. The search strategy included multiple databases, such as the Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group's Trials Register, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, and Web of Science, covering studies published up to January 2014. The inclusion criteria were randomized and controlled clinical trials involving adolescents aged 13 to 18 years, comparing maintenance pharmacological interventions with other treatments or no treatment. Two trials involving a total of 189 participants met the inclusion criteria. The first study, with 35 participants, compared methadone with levo-alpha-acetylmethadol (LAAM) for a 16-week maintenance period followed by detoxification. The second study, with 154 participants, compared buprenorphine-naloxone maintenance treatment with buprenorphine detoxification. Due to differences in the interventions studied, a meta-analysis was not performed. In the methadone versus LAAM study, no significant differences were observed in substance use or social functioning between the two groups. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. No adverse effects, such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, weakness, or fatigue, were reported by participants. In the buprenorphine maintenance versus detoxification study, maintenance treatment was more effective in retaining patients in treatment, with a lower risk of dropout (risk ratio [RR] 0.37; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.26 to 0.54). However, there was no significant difference in the number of patients with positive urine tests for opioids at the end of the study (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.22). At one-year follow-up, self-reported opioid use was significantly lower in the maintenance group, although both groups reported high levels of opioid use (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95). Additionally, more patients in the maintenance group were enrolled in other addiction treatment programs at 12 months (RR 1.33; 95% CI 0.94 to 1.88). The quality of evidence for this study was also rated as low. No serious side effects related to buprenorphine-naloxone were reported, and no participants were withdrawn from the study due to adverse effects. The most commonly reported side effect was headache, affecting 16% to 21% of participants in both groups. The authors concluded that it is challenging to draw definitive conclusions based on only two trials. The limited evidence may be due to the practical and ethical difficulties of conducting trials with adolescents. There is an urgent need for further randomized controlled trials comparing maintenance treatments with detoxification or psychosocial interventions. Future studies should include long-term follow-up and assess relapse rates after treatment, as well as social functioning outcomes such as school or work integration and family relationships.
